Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G8. Score fusion relies on test-set statistics and fixed weights; hyper-parameters are under-ablated: Numerous design choices (gamma = 0.1, lambda = 1.0, four feature levels, input resolution 240, learning rate 1e-3, 50 epochs, fixed prompt templates) are presented without sensitivity analysis. In the few-shot branch fusion, the paper describes adding scores on different scales; the released code instead min-max normalises each branch using the minimum and maximum over the ENTIRE TEST SET before fusing them with a fixed weight of 0.5. This normalisation is transductive: it cannot score a single incoming image, and the fused score of an image changes with the composition (e.g. prevalence, outliers) of the rest of the test set.
- G9. Image-level aggregation is inconsistent and outlier-sensitive: The image-level score is computed differently in training and testing and across datasets: training mean-pools the detection map; for datasets with masks, the reported image AUC uses the MAX over the fused segmentation map, so a single spurious high-scoring pixel decides the image label; for datasets without masks, mean-pooled detection scores are used. No robust aggregation, calibration or uncertainty estimate is used.
- G11. Metrics are too narrow for clinical readiness: Only image-level and pixel-level AUC are reported. The paper does not report Dice, IoU, or PRO scores; thresholded accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV; false positives per patient; calibration or expected calibration error (ECE); or prevalence-adjusted and rare-category performance. AUC alone can obscure poor performance under severe class imbalance and does not by itself demonstrate clinical utility.
- G17. Paper and code disagree on image-level pooling: Eq. (3) of the paper defines the image-level loss with a max over the h x w anomaly map, while the released code mean-pools. Results in the paper therefore cannot be attributed to the method as described, and the effect of the pooling choice on detection is unknown.
